pages.title: Why knifes can be a word
pages.c: **A word form depends on its grammatical role.** Knives is the plural of the noun knife, but knifes is a valid present-tense form of the verb knife. In He knifes him, the singular subject requires a third-person singular verb. The apparent Scrabble disagreement disappears once the noun and verb uses are distinguished.
support: Using knife as a verb is zero derivation, which creates a word in a different category without adding a derivational affix. Adding the final -s to that verb is inflection. The example therefore combines creation of a verb from a noun with the grammatical marking required by the sentence.
pages.d: The spelling knifes cannot be judged independently of its use. It is not the noun’s irregular plural, but it is the verb form required after he in the present tense. Derivation supplies the verb knife, and inflection supplies knifes for its role in that sentence.
pages.visual: The dialogue contrasts knife as an object with knife as an action. The final sentence includes a singular subject, an inflected verb, and an object, so the grammatical context explains the disputed ending.

pages.title: Morphemes and derivation
pages.c: **Derivational morphology builds new words from meaningful parts called morphemes.** In morphology, morph- contributes the idea of form and -ology contributes the idea of a field of study. Combining them produces a word about the study of word forms. This illustrates how a complex word can contain parts that recur in other words.
support: A morpheme is not the same thing as a syllable or an individual speech sound. The relevant unit contributes meaning or grammatical information. Derivation concerns the ways such units combine or change category to create a new lexical item.
pages.d: Understanding a complex word often involves recognizing reusable meaningful components. The analysis of morph- and -ology shows how those components jointly contribute to a larger word. Derivational morphology describes this creation of lexical forms from existing material.
pages.visual: The written decomposition places morph- and -ology on either side of a plus sign. The result connects the two contributions to the meaning of morphology rather than treating the word as an unanalyzed string.

pages.title: Derived meanings are partly conventional
pages.c: **The meaning of a derived word is not always fully predictable from the meaning of its base.** Turning knife into a verb selects a particular action associated with knives rather than every possible use of every object called a knife. Derivation can extend existing vocabulary while relying on conventional knowledge about what the new form ordinarily means.
support: The pictures include different cutting implements, tableware, and an improvised weapon. A noun can apply to a range of objects, while the related verb emphasizes a narrower kind of action. This difference shows why changing grammatical category also requires interpreting how the base meaning is being used.
pages.d: A noun-to-verb conversion can keep the same visible form while changing which aspect of the concept matters. Knife as a noun names an implement, whereas knife as a verb selects a particular action. The relation is understandable, but the verb does not simply inherit every possible property or use of the noun.
pages.visual: The varied implements make the category-to-action distinction concrete. Objects can resemble one another in being cutting tools without being equally natural examples of the action described by the verb knife.

pages.title: The productivity of -hood
pages.c: **A productive derivational pattern can still have restrictions and established exceptions.** The suffix -hood appears in brotherhood, sisterhood, and knighthood, but its contribution is not identical in each word. Brotherhood can describe a shared relation among brothers, while knighthood describes a status held by a knight.
support: Neighborhood is an established word, but its meaning is not simply the state of being a neighbor in the same way as the other examples. Friendhood is not the conventional English form because friendship is used instead. A recognizable affix therefore does not combine equally naturally with every semantically plausible base.
pages.d: Productivity means a pattern can support word formation, not that every possible combination is an equally established word. The -hood examples show both meaning variation among existing forms and gaps where a different form is conventional. Knowing an affix includes learning how its uses are distributed.
pages.visual: The starred examples serve different purposes. Neighborhood is explicitly a valid word with a different interpretation of the pattern, whereas friendhood and enemyhood are proposed formations that contrast with established alternatives. The star is not doing one uniform job across the list.

pages.title: Zero derivation and conventional meaning
pages.c: **Zero derivation changes a word’s category without adding a visible affix, but the resulting meaning can be complex.** A noun such as dish or table can have a related verb use whose interpretation is not obtained by simply naming the object. She can dish it out and They decided to table the issue depend on learned uses of the derived verbs.
support: Associations among knife, dish, spoon, fork, and table do not make their corresponding uses semantically interchangeable. Forked tongue also combines a familiar object-related shape with an established figurative interpretation. Lexical relationships connect meanings without making the outcome of every conversion mechanically predictable.
pages.d: Changing category can select an action, a relation, or a figurative interpretation associated with a base word. The important point is that an unchanged word form does not imply unchanged meaning. Conventional usage helps determine what a converted form communicates in its sentence.
pages.visual: The examples place familiar object words inside different sentence contexts. Reading them as literal references to utensils or furniture would miss the intended meanings of dish it out, forked tongue, and table the issue.

pages.title: Derivation can change pronunciation
pages.c: **Adding derivational material can change the pronunciation of the existing word as well as adding sounds.** Certificate, certification, and recertification differ in their stress patterns and in aspects of their vowels. The phonological form of a derived word is therefore not always a base pronunciation followed by a completely independent ending.
support: The noun and verb uses of record and invite further illustrate a relationship between grammatical category and stress. The marked syllables shift in prominence even when the written form is unchanged. The two uses of entrance also contrast in pronunciation, although their similar spelling does not establish the same derivational relationship.
pages.d: Morphological structure and phonology interact. A derived form may reorganize stress, which can also affect how its syllables are pronounced. The certificate family makes this interaction visible across affixed forms, while record and invite make it visible across noun and verb uses.
pages.visual: The IPA stress marks identify prominent syllables within the transcriptions. Comparing their positions across certificate, certification, and recertification reveals that the change extends into the word’s overall stress pattern.

pages.title: Inflection adds grammatical information
pages.c: **Inflection changes a word’s grammatical form while preserving its identity as the same lexical item.** Plural nouns, third-person singular present-tense verbs, and past-tense verbs illustrate this kind of change. Knife and knives are singular and plural forms of one noun, while knife, knifes, and knifed are different grammatical forms of the verb.
support: The grammatical interpretation can be predictable even when the sound change is irregular. Mouse becomes mice, and sing becomes sang, but the plural and past-tense contributions remain identifiable. Regular endings and irregular changes can therefore perform the same grammatical function.
pages.d: Inflection expresses distinctions such as number, agreement, and tense. It does not require a new unrelated dictionary meaning for each form. Forks and mice both mark plural number despite their different sound patterns, just as walked and sang both express past tense.
pages.visual: The three example groups separate plural formation, present-tense agreement, and past tense. Within each group, regular and irregular pairs illustrate a shared grammatical contribution achieved through different phonological changes.

pages.title: Syntax can require inflection
pages.c: **The grammatical context can require a particular inflected form.** In an ordinary counting expression beginning with two, a following count noun must express plural number. The requirement holds whether the noun forms its plural regularly, as in forks, or irregularly, as in knives.
support: Derivation does not operate under the same requirement. A pattern such as Once you verb it, you can un-verb it may suggest a possible word formation, but the sentence does not grammatically require every verb to have an un- derivative. Syntax can require inflection even when derivation remains lexically restricted.
pages.d: The distinction is between a grammatical obligation and a possible new word. Two creates a number requirement for the noun phrase. Adding un- instead depends on whether a particular derived verb exists or makes sense in the intended use. These are different kinds of constraints.
pages.visual: The expression two [noun]+pl represents a slot with a plural requirement. Different nouns can fill that slot, and each supplies its own appropriate plural form. The slot’s grammatical requirement remains constant across those choices.

pages.title: Inflection differs across languages
pages.c: **Languages differ in how much grammatical information they express through inflection.** English marks some distinctions in noun number and verb tense or agreement, but other languages use more extensive systems. Their word forms can distinguish additional person, tense, number, or case information.
support: Some languages distinguish different quantities through their number system, conjugate verbs for more person or tense combinations, or mark nouns for case. Case marking expresses information about a noun’s syntactic or semantic role. English therefore illustrates inflection without representing the full range of grammatical marking found across languages.
pages.d: Inflection is a general linguistic process whose particular categories vary across languages. The English plural and tense examples provide familiar cases, while richer person, number, tense, and case systems show how much more grammatical information a language can encode within word forms.
pages.visual: The English examples occupy one side of the comparison, while the other lists additional inflectional distinctions found across languages. The comparison concerns the grammatical work performed by word forms, not whether one language has more vocabulary than another.

pages.title: Distinguishing derivation and inflection
pages.c: **Derivation creates lexical items, while inflection supplies grammatical forms used in syntactic contexts.** Both processes build forms from existing material and affect interpretation. They differ in the kind of change they make. A derived word can have a new category or a partly conventional meaning, whereas an inflected form expresses a grammatical distinction associated with the same lexical item.
support: Productivity and regularity are separate issues. Derivational patterns may extend to new words while remaining restricted. Inflection can be broadly required by grammar while using irregular sound changes. The knife examples illustrate both distinctions within one family of forms.
pages.d: Identify what a morphological change accomplishes. If it creates a new lexical use, such as the verb knife from the noun, it is derivational. If it marks the form needed for a sentence, such as knifes after he, it is inflectional. Sound regularity alone cannot decide between them.
pages.visual: The comparison separates three points about inflection—syntactic interaction, broad productivity, and possible irregularity—from the creation and restricted productivity associated with derivation. These properties should be compared independently.

pages.title: Content words and function words
pages.c: **Phrases combine content words with words that organize their grammatical relationships.** Nouns and verbs are content-word classes, as are adjectives and adverbs. Determiners and prepositions help specify how those content words function together. Understanding a sentence therefore requires more than identifying the meanings of its nouns and verbs.
support: In The video for “More than Words” came out before most of you were born, the subject is a whole noun phrase rather than just the isolated noun video. The song title contributes to identifying which video is meant, while function words connect that identifying material to the noun.
pages.d: A phrase is an organized group of words that can function as a unit. Content words contribute much of the descriptive meaning, and function words help establish the structure. The video for “More than Words” shows how several words can jointly identify a single subject.
pages.visual: The curly brackets group The video for “More than Words” and most of you as noun phrases. Their different lengths show that a phrase category is not defined by a fixed number of words.

pages.title: The structure of a noun phrase
pages.c: **The video for “More than Words” is a noun phrase with a determiner, a head noun, and a prepositional phrase.** The specifies the noun phrase, video is its head, and for “More than Words” adds information about which video is meant. The entire phrase can act as a unit in a sentence.
support: The preposition for introduces the modifying phrase. The quoted song title functions as the expression naming the song, so its internal words are not being used as an ordinary unquoted sequence in this sentence. The analysis depends on grammatical function rather than simply on how many words appear.
pages.d: The structure can be summarized as Det + N + PP. This identifies a pattern shared by noun phrases with different vocabulary. The head noun anchors the phrase, while the determiner and the prepositional phrase help specify its reference.
pages.visual: Det abbreviates determiner, N abbreviates noun, and PP abbreviates prepositional phrase. The plus signs indicate how these constituents combine into the larger noun phrase rather than assigning every word the same structural status.

pages.title: Abstract phrase structure across different words
pages.c: **Different expressions can share an abstract organization even when their words and lengths differ.** Two guys from the early ’nineties and a band with only one hit both contain a determiner, a head noun, and a modifying prepositional phrase. One and only one phrase unrelated to early ’nineties one-hit wonder Extreme also has a determiner, head noun, and modifier, although its modifier is an adjective phrase containing a prepositional phrase.
support: The level of abstraction matters because a structural description identifies relationships among categories. A determiner can contain several words, as in one and only one. The head noun still identifies the kind of entity being described.

In the longest example, unrelated heads the adjective phrase, and the expression beginning with to is its prepositional complement. Recognizing the broad head–modifier pattern still leaves room to distinguish the grammatical category of each particular modifier.
pages.d: First find the head nouns guys, band, and phrase. Then separate each determiner from the following modifier. From the early ’nineties and with only one hit are prepositional phrases. Unrelated to early ’nineties one-hit wonder Extreme is an adjective phrase with a prepositional phrase inside it. The examples share a broader organization while their modifiers have different internal structures.
pages.visual: The aligned examples place two, a, and one and only one before the head nouns guys, band, and phrase. The first two following modifiers begin with the prepositions from and with. The third begins with the adjective unrelated, followed by a to phrase. The alignment makes the common positions visible while the words identify the modifier categories.

pages.title: Comparing noun phrases across languages
pages.c: **Abstract phrase categories make it possible to compare different word orders across languages.** The English phrase the cat in the coffee shop places the modifying expression after cat. In the Chinese example 咖啡店裡面的小貓, the location expression precedes the noun. Both expressions identify the cat through its relationship to a coffee shop.
support: The Chinese example also lacks a separate determiner corresponding to English the. A learner must therefore acquire more than individual word translations when moving between the two languages. The category noun phrase can be shared while its internal arrangement and grammatical requirements differ.
pages.d: Cross-language comparison requires separating a phrase’s function from its surface order. The same referent can be described by an English noun followed by a location phrase or by a Chinese expression in which the location comes first. A common phrase category permits the similarities and differences to be stated together.
pages.visual: The gloss coffeeshop inside + cat makes the ordering contrast explicit. The English translation includes the and places in the coffee shop after cat, so the comparison concerns both constituent order and determiner use.

pages.title: Prepositional phrases contain noun phrases
pages.c: **A prepositional phrase commonly contains a preposition followed by a noun phrase.** From the early ’nineties and with only one hit differ in their words, but both combine a relational element with a nominal expression. This gives the broad pattern P + NP.
support: The noun phrase inside a prepositional phrase can itself contain several components. In the early ’nineties, the functions as a determiner, early modifies the noun, and ’nineties names the period. A compact structural label can therefore stand for a larger internal organization.
pages.d: The P + NP pattern treats the noun phrase as one constituent even when it contains multiple words. This is useful because a preposition relates that whole constituent to the rest of the expression. Describing only a flat string would conceal the grouping.
pages.visual: The braces around the early ’nineties identify it as the NP attached to from. The outer combination creates a PP, while the inner Det + Adj + N analysis describes the structure within the NP.

pages.title: Phrase structure is hierarchical
pages.c: **A sentence has constituents inside other constituents.** In from the early ’nineties, the determiner, adjective, and noun belong inside a noun phrase. That noun phrase then belongs inside a prepositional phrase. The prepositional phrase can in turn modify a noun within an even larger expression.
support: A tree diagram represents this nesting by giving each constituent a node above the parts it contains. Words that sit next to one another in the spoken sequence can therefore participate in different levels of structure. The hierarchical grouping helps explain which parts act together as a unit.
pages.d: Hierarchy means that a phrase can be treated as a unit at one level while being analyzed into smaller units at another. The NP in a PP is both a whole constituent and an internally structured expression. A tree makes these nested relationships visible without flattening them into one row.
pages.visual: The tree branches from a sentence node into phrase nodes and then into smaller categories and words. The branch structure represents containment. It is the relation among those nodes, rather than the visual spacing of individual words, that carries the grammatical analysis.

pages.title: Verb phrases can contain different complements
pages.c: **A verb phrase combines a verb with material that completes or expands its predicate.** Sang the song contains a verb and a noun phrase. Threw a party for him combines a verb, an object noun phrase, and a prepositional phrase. Verb phrases can therefore differ in internal structure while serving the same broad sentence function.
support: Worked himself to death includes both a noun phrase and a following expression describing the result. Came out before most of you were born includes material locating the event in time. Identifying the whole predicate helps keep these related pieces together rather than treating the verb as the entire phrase.
pages.d: A verb can organize several kinds of accompanying material. The examples contrast a verb with an NP, a verb with a temporal expression, and a verb with both an NP and a PP. The predicate’s structure depends on how these constituents relate to the event being expressed.
pages.visual: The braces group the song, a party, and for him into constituents. The formulas V + NP and V + NP + PP summarize the relations among those groups. Each abbreviation stands for a grammatical unit that may contain several words.

pages.title: Subjects and predicates
pages.c: **A clause pairs a predicate with its subject.** In The video for “More than Words” came out before most of you were born, the main subject is the whole noun phrase beginning with the video. Video is the head noun within that subject. The main predicate describes the event of the video coming out.
support: The subject is identified through its grammatical relationship to the predicate, rather than simply by picking the first noun encountered. Words inside a modifying phrase help identify the subject’s referent without replacing the head noun as the organizer of the main noun phrase.
pages.d: The whole subject phrase and its head noun play related but different roles. The phrase The video for “More than Words” occupies the subject position, while video is its head. The remaining main predicate tells what happened to that referent.
pages.visual: The bracketing separates a large NP from the following predicate. Inside that NP, Det + N + PP groups the determiner, head noun, and modifier. The nested structure explains why the song title does not become the main subject.

pages.title: Agreement follows the head of the subject
pages.c: **The main verb agrees with the head of its subject noun phrase.** In The plums in the icebox were delicious, plums is plural, so the predicate uses were. Icebox is a singular noun inside a modifying phrase, but it does not control the main verb’s agreement.
support: Adding which you were probably saving for breakfast introduces another subject–verb relationship within the sentence. You controls were saving, while plums still controls were delicious. Replacing you with my roommate changes the embedded verb to was saving without changing the main plural agreement.
pages.d: Agreement reveals which noun phrase controls which verb. A nearby singular noun such as icebox does not override the plural head plums. An embedded clause creates its own local subject–verb relation, so changing that embedded subject affects its own verb rather than every verb in the sentence.
pages.visual: The contrasting sentences place extra material between plums and were delicious. Their shared main agreement demonstrates that grammatical control depends on structure rather than on choosing the closest preceding noun. Forgive me additionally illustrates a subject understood from context rather than overtly spoken.

pages.title: Active and passive syntax
pages.c: **The same event can be expressed with different syntactic subjects.** In I have eaten the plums in the icebox, I is the subject and the plums in the icebox is the object. In The plums in the icebox were eaten by me, the plums in the icebox becomes the subject. The passive sentence’s plural agreement provides evidence for that subject assignment.
support: The phrase by me identifies the person who performed the action, but it is a prepositional phrase rather than the grammatical subject. This distinction prevents the meaning-based question of who acted from being substituted for the structural question of which phrase controls the verb.
pages.d: Active and passive sentences rearrange grammatical roles while describing the same eating event. The person who ate the plums is the subject in the active sentence. The affected plums become the subject in the passive sentence, while by me identifies the actor within a PP.
pages.visual: The forms have eaten and were eaten occur with different subjects. The plural were matches plums in the passive sentence. The bracketed by me phrase retains the actor’s identity without occupying the subject position.

pages.title: Semantic roles remain stable across voice
pages.c: **Semantic roles identify how participants contribute to an event.** In the plum example, the eater is the agent, the plums are the undergoer, and the icebox supplies the location. These event roles remain the same whether the sentence uses an active or passive construction.
support: A syntactic subject is therefore not always the agent. I is both subject and agent in the active version, but the plums are subject and undergoer in the passive version. Distinguishing these two descriptions makes it possible to explain what changes in the sentence structure and what remains constant in the event.
pages.d: Ask two separate questions about each participant. Its semantic role concerns the event, such as acting or being affected. Its syntactic role concerns the grammatical construction, such as subject or object. Changing voice can alter the second answer while preserving the first.
pages.visual: The passive mapping is Undergoer + Location + Verb + Agent. The active mapping is Agent + Verb + Undergoer + Location. The order changes, but the eater, affected plums, and location keep the same event roles.

pages.title: Language combines structure at several levels
pages.c: **Language is generative because familiar elements can be combined into new words and new expressions.** Derivational morphology creates lexical forms, syntax organizes words into larger structures, and inflection marks words for grammatical requirements. These processes let speakers produce and understand expressions they have not memorized as complete wholes.
support: Much of this organization operates without explicit reflection. A speaker can select a plural, construct a phrase, or interpret a passive sentence without naming the relevant grammatical categories. Linguistic analysis makes these ordinary but complex abilities available for explanation.
pages.d: Word formation, grammatical marking, and phrase structure contribute different kinds of organization. Their interaction supports the creation of meaningful new utterances from familiar material. The ability feels ordinary because speakers use it fluently, even though its underlying structure is complex.
pages.visual: The summary distinguishes new-word creation, syntactic combination, and grammatical modification. Keeping those processes separate clarifies how a sentence can simultaneously involve derivation, inflection, and hierarchical organization.

questions.stem: Why is knifes appropriate in He knifes him even though the noun plural is knives?
choices: Knife has been used as a verb, and its third-person singular present form takes -s.
The irregular noun plural becomes regular whenever the noun follows he.
Knifes is a plural noun functioning as the subject of the sentence.
Every derivational process adds an audible affix.
questions.why: Zero derivation supplies the verb knife. Its agreement form knifes is an inflection, whereas knives is the plural noun form.

questions.stem: What do the -hood examples demonstrate about derivational productivity?
choices: A pattern can support word formation while retaining lexical restrictions and meaning differences.
A productive suffix must combine with every noun in exactly the same way.
Neighborhood is not an English word because it is marked with a star.
Friendship is an inflected form of friendhood.
questions.why: Brotherhood, knighthood, neighborhood, and friendship show that the availability and meaning of derived forms are partly conventional.

questions.stem: Why are certificate, certification, and recertification useful for studying morphology and phonology together?
choices: Adding derivational material can reorganize stress and pronunciation within the word.
Their grammatical differences occur only in spelling and never in speech.
They prove that each added affix leaves the base pronunciation untouched.
They demonstrate plural number agreement with a preceding determiner.
questions.why: The stress patterns differ across the related forms. Derivation can affect the phonological organization of the base as well as adding material.

questions.stem: What do forks and mice have in common despite their different sound changes?
choices: Both express plural number through inflection.
Both are created by changing a noun into a verb.
Both use the same regular plural suffix in pronunciation.
Both require a new unrelated lexical meaning for the plural.
questions.why: Plural number is the shared grammatical contribution. Forks uses a regular ending and mice an irregular change, so grammatical function does not require identical phonology.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the plural requirement in two knives from a possible un- derivative?
choices: The syntactic number context requires a plural, while derivation depends on whether an appropriate lexical formation is available.
The plural is optional, while every English verb must take un-.
Both require exactly the same phonological ending on the base.
Neither is related to grammar or meaning.
questions.why: Syntax imposes the plural requirement in an ordinary counting phrase. Derivational possibility is not the same kind of grammatical obligation.

questions.stem: Why can two guys from the early ’nineties and a band with only one hit share a structural description?
choices: Both can be analyzed as determiner + head noun + prepositional phrase despite different vocabulary.
They contain exactly the same number of words in each constituent.
Every word in either phrase has the same grammatical category.
Their meanings must be identical because their phrase structures are comparable.
questions.why: Abstract phrase structure captures category relationships that recur across different words, meanings, and constituent lengths.

questions.stem: What does a phrase-structure tree represent that a flat word list does not?
choices: Constituents nested inside larger constituents.
Only the chronological order in which the speaker learned the words.
A requirement that every noun phrase contains exactly three words.
The sound frequency of each spoken word.
questions.why: A tree represents hierarchical containment, such as an NP inside a PP that can itself modify a larger NP.

questions.stem: Why is were appropriate in The plums in the icebox were delicious?
choices: The plural head plums controls the main predicate’s agreement.
The closest noun icebox controls the verb but is interpreted as plural.
Any noun inside a prepositional phrase overrides the head noun.
The agent of an eating event must always determine grammatical number.
questions.why: The subject phrase is headed by plums. The singular icebox occurs inside a modifier and does not control the main verb.

questions.stem: In The plums in the icebox were eaten by me, which phrase is the grammatical subject?
choices: The plums in the icebox.
By me.
Were eaten.
In the icebox alone.
questions.why: The plums in the icebox is the subject and its plural head agrees with were. By me expresses the agent inside a prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: What remains stable when I have eaten the plums becomes The plums were eaten by me?
choices: The eater remains the agent and the plums remain the undergoer.
The same phrase remains the grammatical subject.
The same phrase remains the grammatical object in both constructions.
The surface order of every constituent remains unchanged.
questions.why: Voice changes syntactic organization while preserving the relevant event roles. The actor and affected participant remain the same.

written.prompt: Use knife, knives, knifes, and knifed to distinguish derivation from inflection and explain the role of syntax.
answer: Turning the noun knife into the verb knife is zero derivation.
Knives marks plural number on the noun, while knifes and knifed mark grammatical forms of the verb.
The singular subject in He knifes him requires the corresponding present-tense agreement form.
Regularity of the sound change does not determine whether the process is inflectional.

written.prompt: Compare I have eaten the plums in the icebox with The plums in the icebox were eaten by me. Identify the syntactic subject, agent, undergoer, and location in each.
answer: I is the active subject, while the plums in the icebox is the passive subject.
The eater is the agent in both versions.
The plums are the undergoer, and the icebox supplies the location.
Passive by me is a prepositional phrase expressing the agent rather than the grammatical subject.
